title: The Company That Wasn't There
subtitle: Germany's proudest technology company was worth more than Deutsche Bank. Then somebody asked two banks a simple question.

vocab.def: Money that goes from one person or company to another. The verb is to pay.
vocab.ex: Wirecard processed payments for online shops.

vocab.def: The crime of lying about money to get money.
vocab.ex: It became the biggest fraud in modern German history.

vocab.def: A person who checks and prepares a company's financial records. The check itself is an audit.
vocab.ex: The accountants signed the accounts every year for a decade.

vocab.def: A person who writes news for a newspaper, a website or television.
vocab.ex: A journalist at the Financial Times reported the story for five years.

vocab.def: To say that something is not true.
A government organisation that controls an industry and makes sure it follows the law.
vocab.ex: The German regulator defended the company.

vocab.def: To try to find out the truth about something.
vocab.ex: The police investigated the journalists, not the company.

vocab.def: To go away suddenly so that nobody can find you.
vocab.ex: One director disappeared and has never been found.

vocab.def: Facts or objects that show whether something is true.
vocab.ex: There was evidence for years, but nobody acted on it.

vocab.def: To fall down suddenly and completely.
vocab.ex: The company collapsed one week later.

vocab_discuss: Do you believe what you read in the newspapers? Always, sometimes, never?
Who should check that big companies are honest? The government, the accountants, or somebody else?
Have you ever been sure about something that everybody else doubted?

story.heading: Part 1 — Germany's champion
paras: Wirecard started in the late 1990s. It processed payments on the internet, for businesses that ordinary banks did not want to talk about.
Slowly it became respectable. It got a banking licence. It got famous customers. And it had a perfect story for its moment.
Germany is an industrial superpower, but it was embarrassed: it had almost no big technology companies. Now here was a German company, near Munich, winning the world's payments business.
Its chief executive, Markus Braun, dressed and spoke like a Silicon Valley boss. He promised big growth every year. On paper, he delivered it every year.

Where did the profit come from? According to the accounts, from partner companies in Asia. In countries where Wirecard had no licence, these partners processed payments for it. The money was said to be sitting in special accounts in the Philippines.
Look carefully at that structure. The company's most profitable business was in other people's companies, in other people's paperwork, in other people's banks.
In 2018 Wirecard reached the top. It entered the DAX, the list of Germany's thirty most valuable companies, and pushed out Commerzbank — a technology company replacing an old bank.
At its highest point it was worth about twenty-four billion euros: more than Deutsche Bank. Politicians promoted it on foreign trips. Investment funds had to buy it.
And all that national pride had quietly become part of the company's defences.
tf: Wirecard was a German company that processed internet payments.
Most of its profit came from its own offices in Germany.
In 2018 it was worth more than Deutsche Bank.
discuss: Why was it useful for Wirecard that Germany wanted a technology champion?
The biggest profits were in other people's companies and banks. Why is that a warning sign?

story.heading: Part 2 — Everybody was told
paras: The extraordinary thing about this fraud is that it was not really hidden. It was published, in a famous newspaper, for years.

From 2015, a Financial Times journalist called Dan McCrum wrote a series of articles about false numbers and strange accounting. Investors who were betting against the company circulated detailed reports. In 2018, employees in Wirecard's own Singapore office reported forged contracts, and the police raided the office there.
Every time, the company did the same four things. It denied everything. It said the journalists and the investors were criminals working together. It went to court. And it announced more growth.
Then came the part that Germany still finds painful.

In February 2019, the German financial regulator did something it had never done before. It banned people from betting against this one company's shares — protecting Wirecard — and it made criminal complaints against the Financial Times journalists.
Think about what that meant. A national regulator had decided that the most likely explanation for detailed evidence of fraud was that a major newspaper was lying.

Meanwhile the accountants had approved the accounts every year for a decade. For the billions in the Philippines, they had relied on documents and letters — they had never gone to the banks themselves and checked that the money was there.
tf: The German regulator investigated the journalists.
The accountants checked directly with the banks that the money existed.
discuss: The regulator protected the company and investigated the newspaper. How could that happen?
Whose job was it to check that the money actually existed?

story.heading: Part 3 — One letter, two banks
paras: Under pressure, Wirecard asked a different firm, KPMG, to do a special check. Their report came in April 2020. It was written in careful, polite language, but the meaning was terrible: for the business that produced most of the profits, they could not confirm that it existed.
Then the end came very fast.
In June 2020 the accountants finally did the obvious thing. They asked for direct confirmation from the two banks in the Philippines that were holding the 1.9 billion euros.
The banks replied that the documents were forgeries and that the accounts did not exist. There was no money. There had never been any money.
On 18 June, Wirecard announced that 1.9 billion euros "probably do not exist". Braun resigned and was arrested within days.

Jan Marsalek, the director responsible for the Asian business, took a private plane out of Austria and disappeared. Reports say he travelled through Belarus into Russia. He is still on Europe's most-wanted list.
One week after the announcement, Wirecard went bankrupt — the first company ever to collapse out of the DAX, about two years after joining it.
Ordinary German savers lost money, because funds that follow the DAX had been forced to own it until days before the end.

Now look at the whole story. On one side: a company that insisted and denied, accountants who confirmed, and a regulator that attacked the critics. On the other: journalists who alleged, employees who reported, and investors who bet against it.
Everyone with official authority pointed one way. Everyone with money at risk and no national pride to protect pointed the other.
And the evidence that ended it was one letter from two banks. Anybody could have asked for it in any of the previous six years.
tf: The 1.9 billion euros was found in a different bank.
Markus Braun was arrested after the announcement.
The decisive evidence was very difficult and expensive to obtain.
discuss: The final proof took one letter. Why did nobody ask for it earlier?
Who is most to blame here: the company, the accountants, or the regulator?
Tell the story in six sentences. Use: claimed · denied · reported · refused · admitted · collapsed.

grammar.name: say, tell, ask
grammar.heading: Reporting what people said: say, tell, ask
explain: This story is about who said what, and who believed them. To retell it you need the three reporting verbs that English students mix up most often.
say — no person after it. → "The company said that the money existed." / "He said to me that…"
tell — always a person after it. → "The journalist told his editor the truth." (NOT told to his editor)
ask — for questions and requests. → "They asked the banks a question."
The one rule to remember: tell needs a person; say does not. tell somebody something · say something (to somebody).
Also useful here: deny + -ing → "He denied knowing about it." And refuse + to → "They refused to answer."

fix.heading: Find the mistake
items: He said me that everything was fine.
She told that the money did not exist.
The journalist asked to the bank a question.
He denied to know anything about the fraud.
The regulator refused believing the newspaper.
answers: He told me that everything was fine. (or: he said to me)
She said that the money did not exist. (tell needs a person)
The journalist asked the bank a question. (no to after ask)
He denied knowing anything about the fraud. (deny + -ing)
The regulator refused to believe the newspaper. (refuse + to + verb)

speak.label: 1 · Tell the story
paras: Tell me the story of Wirecard in your own words. Six or seven sentences is enough.

speak.label: 2 · Nobody believed you
paras: Tell me about a time you were right and nobody believed you.
What happened in the end?

speak.label: 3 · Who do you trust?
paras: Put these in order of how much you trust them: a newspaper, an accountant, a government regulator, a company's own boss.
Explain your order.

speak.label: 4 · Your opinion
paras: Germany wanted a technology champion very badly. Did that make the fraud easier?
Is national pride dangerous in business?

final: How do you decide whether a news story is true?
Should the people who checked the accounts go to prison, or just lose their jobs?
Is there a company in your country that everybody admires? What would happen if it failed?
